`git rebase --onto` transplants a range of commits onto a new base. You pick the range explicitly, so you can move commits that a plain `git rebase` would drag along or leave behind.

**Syntax**

```
git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [<branch>]
```

Git takes the commits that are in `<branch>` (default: current branch) but not in `<upstream>`. It replays them on top of `<newbase>`.

**Example**

Say `feature-b` was branched off `feature-a`, which was branched off `main`:

```
main:       A---B
                 \
feature-a:        C---D
                       \
feature-b:              E---F
```

You want `feature-b` to depend only on `main`, not on `feature-a`'s commits (`C` and `D`):

```
git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b
```

Here `feature-a` is the upstream, so the range is `feature-a..feature-b`, which is `E` and `F`. Those are replayed onto `main`:

```
main:       A---B---E'---F'   (feature-b)
                 \
feature-a:        C---D
```

`E'` and `F'` are new commits with new hashes, with the same changes as `E` and `F`.

**Common uses**

- **Move a branch to a different base**, as above.
- **Drop commits from the middle of a branch.** `git rebase --onto HEAD~3 HEAD~1` removes the two commits just before the tip. The range is `HEAD~1..HEAD`, so only the tip is replayed onto `HEAD~3`.
- **Recover after the parent branch was squash-merged.** Your branch still carries the old commits of the parent. Use `git rebase --onto main <old-parent-tip> my-branch` to bring over only your own commits.

Since `rebase --onto` rewrites history, avoid it on commits others have already pulled. If you push afterward, use `git push --force-with-lease`.
